sumer.name: Sumer
sumer.summary: The earliest known civilization, in southern Mesopotamia (now south-central Iraq), emerging between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE; its cities produced the world's earliest known written texts.

pre-pottery-neolithic-a.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA)
pre-pottery-neolithic-a.summary: The first stage of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic in the Levant and Anatolia, dating to about 10,000-8,800 BCE, marked by small circular mud-brick dwellings and early crop cultivation.

pre-pottery-neolithic-b.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB)
pre-pottery-neolithic-b.summary: The second stage of the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, centred in upper Mesopotamia and the Levant from about 8,800 to 6,500 BC, developing from the earlier PPNA culture with likely influence from northeastern Anatolia.

tell-abu-hureyra.name: Tell Abu Hureyra
tell-abu-hureyra.summary: A prehistoric site in Syria's Upper Euphrates valley where hunter-gatherers gradually became some of the world's first farmers, notably cultivating rye.

mureybet.name: Mureybet
mureybet.summary: An ancient settlement mound on the Euphrates in northern Syria, occupied from about 10,200 to 8000 BC and the type site for the early-farming Mureybetian culture.

natufian-culture.name: Natufian culture
natufian-culture.summary: Archaeological culture of the late Epipalaeolithic Near East, from about 15,000 to 11,500 years ago, notable for supporting settled communities before agriculture and producing some of the earliest known bread and beer.

jarmo.name: Jarmo
jarmo.summary: A prehistoric agricultural settlement in the Zagros foothills of modern Iraqi Kurdistan, dating to around 7090 BC and roughly contemporary with Jericho and Çatalhöyük.

zagros-mountains.name: Zagros Mountains
zagros-mountains.summary: A 1,600 km mountain range spanning Iran, northern Iraq, and southeastern Turkey, running from Iran's western border to the Persian Gulf.

hassuna-culture.name: Hassuna culture
hassuna-culture.summary: A Neolithic archaeological culture in northern Mesopotamia dating to the early sixth millennium BC, named after the type site of Tell Hassuna in Iraq.

epic-of-gilgamesh.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
epic-of-gilgamesh.summary: The world's oldest surviving work of narrative literature, from ancient Mesopotamia, telling of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and his companion Enkidu; its standard version dates to the 13th–10th centuries BCE.

enkidu.name: Enkidu
enkidu.summary: Legendary wild man and comrade of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, in the Epic of Gilgamesh; the oldest literary depiction of the 'wild man' figure.

gilgamesh.name: Gilgamesh
gilgamesh.summary: Hero of Mesopotamian mythology and protagonist of the Epic of Gilgamesh, possibly a real king of Uruk around 2900–2350 BCE who was later worshipped as a god.

samarra-culture.name: Samarra culture
samarra-culture.summary: A Late Neolithic culture of northern Mesopotamia, roughly 5500 to 4800 BCE, known for finely painted pottery and later succeeded by the Ubaid culture.

ubaid-period.name: Ubaid period
ubaid-period.summary: A prehistoric period of Mesopotamia lasting roughly from 6500 to 3800 BC, marking the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian alluvial plain.

uruk-period.name: Uruk period
uruk-period.summary: The era, roughly 4000 to 3100 BC, when the first cities and states arose in Mesopotamia, named after the city of Uruk where innovations like the potter's wheel appeared.

tell-hassuna.name: Tell Hassuna
tell-hassuna.summary: A settlement mound in Iraq that gives its name to the early sixth-millennium BCE Hassuna culture.

uruk-trough.name: Uruk Trough
uruk-trough.summary: An ancient Sumerian limestone carving from Uruk, Iraq, showing a procession of sheep, among the earliest surviving works of narrative relief sculpture, dated to 3300–3000 BC.

inanna.name: Inanna (Ishtar)
inanna.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian goddess of war, love and sex, originally worshipped in Sumer and later known as Ishtar among the Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians.

mask-of-warka.name: Mask of Warka
mask-of-warka.summary: A carved marble face of a goddess, likely Inanna, from around 3100 BCE and one of the earliest known depictions of a human face; recovered undamaged after being looted from Iraq's National Museum in 2003.

bouqras.name: Bouqras
bouqras.summary: A large prehistoric Neolithic settlement mound near Deir ez-Zor in Syria, notable for early stone containers linked to the development of Mesopotamian art.

tell-es-sawwan.name: Tell es-Sawwan
tell-es-sawwan.summary: An archaeological site on the Tigris River in Iraq that serves as the type site for the Samarra culture.

choga-mami.name: Choga Mami
choga-mami.summary: A Samarran-period settlement in eastern Iraq, notable for the earliest known canal irrigation in operation, around 6000 BCE.

uruk.name: Uruk
uruk.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian city that, at its peak around 3100 BC, may have been the largest urban settlement in the world, with tens of thousands of residents.

eanna.name: Eanna District
eanna.summary: A monumental Sumerian temple complex at Uruk, regarded as the residence of the goddess Inanna and one of ancient Mesopotamia's most influential religious sites.

hamoukar.name: Hamoukar
hamoukar.summary: A large archaeological site in northeastern Syria dating to the 5th millennium BCE, a major center of obsidian production and one of the largest early cities of Northern Mesopotamia.

nemrut-volcano.name: Mount Nemrut
nemrut-volcano.summary: A dormant volcano in eastern Turkey near Lake Van, named after King Nimrod, with a crater lake and a history of eruptions into the Holocene.

ur.name: Ur
ur.summary: A major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia dating from about 3800 BC, whose patron deity was the moon god Nanna and whose ziggurat still stands partially restored.

cuneiform.name: Cuneiform
cuneiform.summary: The earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay, developed for Sumerian and later adapted for Akkadian and other ancient Near Eastern languages.

neba-a-faour.name: Tell Neba'a Faour
neba-a-faour.summary: A low-lying archaeological mound in Lebanon's Bekaa Valley inhabited in the late 7th and early 6th millennium BC, seen as an example of a Pre-Pottery Neolithic C stage.

beqaa-valley.name: Beqaa Valley
beqaa-valley.summary: A fertile farming valley in eastern Lebanon, about 30 km east of Beirut, corresponding to the ancient region of Coele-Syria.

yarim-tepe.name: Yarim Tepe
yarim-tepe.summary: Archaeological site in northern Iraq's Sinjar valley dating to about 6000 BC, reflecting the Hassuna, Halaf, and Ubaid farming cultures.

cylinder-seal.name: Cylinder seal
cylinder-seal.summary: Small engraved cylinder rolled onto wet clay to leave an impression, invented around 3500 BC in the Near East and linked to the development of cuneiform writing.

naqada-culture.name: Naqada culture
naqada-culture.summary: A Chalcolithic Predynastic Egyptian culture (about 4000–3000 BC) named for the town of Naqada, spanning phases Naqada I, II and III with early craft specialization and trade.

tell-el-oueili.name: Tell el-'Oueili
tell-el-oueili.summary: An archaeological site in southern Iraq near Larsa, home to the earliest known Ubaid settlement in Lower Mesopotamia.

larsa.name: Larsa
larsa.summary: An ancient Sumerian city-state near Uruk in what is now Iraq, center of the sun god Utu's cult and a source of Babylonian mathematical tablets.

naqada-ii.name: Naqada II
naqada-ii.summary: The second Predynastic phase of Egypt's Naqada culture, dated to roughly 3500–3300 BC, previously called the Gerzeh (Gerzean) culture after a site studied by Flinders Petrie.

jemdet-nasr.name: Jemdet Nasr
jemdet-nasr.summary: A Sumerian settlement mound in Iraq's Babil Governorate, giving its name to the Jemdet Nasr period (c. 3100–2900 BC); excavations there uncovered early proto-cuneiform tablets.

susa.name: Susa
susa.summary: Ancient city in what is now Iran that served as capital of Elam and winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire, remaining strategically important through the Parthian and Sasanian periods.

urfa-man.name: Urfa Man
urfa-man.summary: A human-shaped stone statue found near Urfa in southeastern Turkey, dated to about 9000 BC and considered the oldest known naturalistic life-sized sculpture of a person.

g-bekli-tepe.name: Göbekli Tepe
g-bekli-tepe.summary: A Neolithic archaeological site in Upper Mesopotamia (modern Turkey), inhabited from about 9500 to at least 8000 BCE, known for huge stone pillars carved with animal and human figures, among the world's oldest megaliths.

pre-pottery-neolithic.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic
pre-pottery-neolithic.summary: The early Neolithic period in the Near East, roughly 12,000 to 8,500 years ago, marking the early stages of plant and animal domestication before pottery came into use.

halaf-culture.name: Halaf culture
halaf-culture.summary: A prehistoric culture lasting from about 6100 to 5100 BCE, centered on the Khabur River valley in what is now southeastern Turkey, Syria and northern Iraq.

khabur.name: Khabur
khabur.summary: The largest perennial tributary of the Euphrates in Syria, originating in Turkey, whose valley has been a vital water source for agriculture throughout history.

tepe-gawra.name: Tepe Gawra
tepe-gawra.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian settlement near Mosul in Iraq, occupied from 5000 to 1500 BC, with remains from the Halaf, Ubaid and Uruk periods.

chagar-bazar.name: Chagar Bazar
chagar-bazar.summary: An ancient settlement mound in northern Syria, occupied from around 6100 BCE to the mid-2nd millennium BCE, where Halaf-period pottery has been found.

ninhursag.name: Ninhursag
ninhursag.summary: Ancient Sumerian mother goddess of the mountains and one of the seven great deities of Sumer, known from myths describing her dealings with the god Enki.

joan-oates.name: Joan Oates
joan-oates.summary: American-British archaeologist specializing in the Ancient Near East, a Cambridge fellow who directed excavations at Tell Brak from 2004.

peter-akkermans.name: Peter Akkermans
peter-akkermans.summary: Dutch archaeologist and professor emeritus at Leiden University, known for excavating Tell Sabi Abyad in northern Syria and studying the Halaf culture.

telul-eth-thalathat.name: Telul eth-Thalathat
telul-eth-thalathat.summary: An ancient Near Eastern site in Iraq with several mounds occupied during the Ubaid, Uruk, and Ninevite 5 periods.
